paper_title: Intergenerational Child Mortality Impacts of Deworming: Experimental Evidence from Two Decades of the Kenya Life Panel Survey
eval_quality_explanation:
The evaluators had clearly engaged seriously with the paper, and provided some helpful feedback. This does not always happen with referee reports. In addition, I felt that evaluators were aiming to be constructive (rather than just critical, which often is the case for referee reports).
The part that is harder to evaluate is that these evaluations are not made in the context of a specific journal, so some of the advice felt beyond the scope of the paper or features that would be nice to have (rather than essential for improving the paper). This contrasts with referee reports where the feedback is often more specific about what would be needed to move the paper over the bar for a particular journal.
engagement_discussion: Evaluators did seem to read the paper closely. Some suggestions were indeed helpful, but others also seemed beyond the scope of the paper.
adaptation_to_eval: Minor: likely to revise small things in response
adaptation_elaboration: We were already in the process of revising the paper when the evaluation took place, so some of the changes that the evaluator’s highlighted were already in the works. There are a couple additional minor changes that we’ll make based on the feedback.

improvement_suggestions: This is tough. I want to see the Unjournal improve, but perhaps by luck of the draw, we ended up getting pretty critical reviews, and those reviews did not move my beliefs about the paper in any way. We also ended up seeming to have a pretty different opinion from David about how to divide our attention between the exploit/explore tradeoff — re: keep improving one paper or start new ones — but this problem has no global solution. So I’m not sure. I’d say in our particular case, I’d suggest seeing the entire thing as an effort to win allies and comrades, and I found the whole experience somewhat alienating. But then again, if the reviewers are right and our paper sucks, then there’s no point worrying about what I think! It really hinges on whether the paper was good or not and whether the reviews were misguided. I think so on both counts 😃 (I would also say that I do not believe the reviewers’ self-claimed credentials at all. One of them said they had worked on hundreds of meta-analyses, which just, no.)

paper_title: The Returns to Science in the Presence of Technological Risk
eval_quality_explanation: I think these generally met or cleared the bar for peer review - but part of that reflects the fact that I think peer review can be pretty superficial.
adaptation_to_eval: Unlikely we will revise anything in response
adaptation_elaboration: It’s a bit misleading when I say that I am unlikely to revise in response to the evaluations; instead, they prompted significant original work which was reflected in my own response to the evaluators. But I felt it worked better as a stand-alone response, then as a revision to the original work. Meanwhile, when I say the evaluations are unlikely to influence my future research, that’s mostly a consequence of the fact that I am not currently in a research position. If I had continued on the research trajectory that was evaluated, I think it would impact things in important ways.
contact_reason: The Unjournal asked me for permission
future_engagement_explanation: Nothing to submit is the most important reason. But I would still not generally consider it because the rewards are too asymmetric and there are opportunity costs. Engaging in the conventional peer review process is a lot of work, but it has a reward at the end of the rainbow - publication in a journal that confers a short-hand signifier of merit to people who are not in a position to independently evaluate the research merits on their own. Meanwhile, conventional peer review caps some of the downside reputational costs by generally not publishing peer review reports (or if they do, its generally after the paper has been accepted, which signals that criticisms of the paper are not fatal). Unfortunately, Unjournal evaluations don’t have these features. The work may be valuable, but I think given opportunity costs, it is unlikely I would voluntarily submit my own work again.
other_comments: The above 90% is my probability of reading at least one more paper at some future point.
improvement_suggestions: I think more awareness for scholars who work in the fields of the reviewed papers is the most important thing to have more impact.
